questions.question: Email outages keep returning even though the service desk restores service for users each time. An IT manager opens a problem record. What is Problem Management's goal in this situation?

options.text: Restore normal service for each affected user quickly
Identify and resolve the underlying cause of outages
Control the life cycle of the changes needed for a fix
Fulfill the catalog requests that affected users submit

explanation.correct: ServiceNow describes Problem Management as having a single goal: identifying and resolving the underlying issues that cause incidents. It is a methodical process in which finding and resolving the root cause matters more than time to resolution, which is exactly what recurring email outages call for once service has been restored each time. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/problem-management/understanding-state-mgmt-transitions.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Restoring normal service while minimizing impact is the purpose of Incident Management, which the service desk is already doing for each outage.
Controlling the life cycle of changes is Change Management. A change request may later be raised to apply the fix, but that is not the problem's goal.
Submitting and fulfilling requests for services and products through a self-service portal is Request Management, not Problem Management.

source.excerpt: Problem Management refers to the process of identifying and resolving the underlying cause of one or more incidents.

questions.question: A problem manager wants the root cause and workaround of a known problem to be searchable so agents can deflect new incidents. They click Create Known Error Article on the problem. Where is the article kept?

options.text: As a work note on each incident related to the problem
In a knowledge base maintained in Knowledge Management
As an attribute on the affected CI record in the CMDB
In a change request raised from the problem record

explanation.correct: Known error articles document the root cause and workaround of a problem to help deflect incidents. When an article is created from a problem, it is saved in the knowledge base and maintained in the Knowledge Management application, where the knowledge base's workflows control publishing and retirement. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/problem-management/create-known-error-from-problem.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Copying text into the work notes of related incidents is what Communicate Workaround does; it notifies existing incidents but does not create a searchable article.
The CMDB associates the problem with affected configuration items, but known error content is not stored on the CI; the article lives in a knowledge base.
A change request from a problem is used to implement the fix to the root cause. It does not store the known error documentation for agents to search.

source.excerpt: The known error database is a repository of problem records that a company has designated as known issues.

questions.question: While assessing a new problem, a problem coordinator finds an existing problem that already covers the same issue. What should the coordinator do with the new problem?

options.text: Click Confirm to start root cause analysis on it
Click Mark Duplicate of the existing problem
Click Cancel because it is not a valid problem
Click Accept Risk to close it without a fix

explanation.correct: In the Assess state, the documented action when there is an existing problem with a similar issue is Mark Duplicate. Marking the problem as a duplicate of an existing problem closes it, and its related records are moved to the existing problem. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/problem-management/assess-a-problem.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Confirm is for a problem that is valid and requires a resolution. It moves the problem to Root Cause Analysis, which would duplicate the work already happening on the existing problem.
Cancel is the documented action when the problem is not a valid problem. Here the issue is real but already covered by another problem.
Accept Risk is used during root cause analysis when there is no permanent resolution to the problem. It is not the way to handle a problem that duplicates another.

source.excerpt: If a problem is detected reactively, it means that one or more incidents have already taken place, prompting an investigation to uncover the root cause of the issue.

questions.question: A problem was closed with the resolution code Fix Applied, but the same incidents have started again. With default Problem Management properties, which role can re-analyze this completed problem?

options.text: problem_task_analyst
problem_coordinator
problem_manager
sn_problem_read

explanation.correct: The property Who can Re-analyze a Completed Problem? (problem.closed.role.reanalyze_from_completed) has the default value problem_manager. Re-analyze reopens the problem and changes its state to Root Cause Analysis. The problem_manager role is responsible for the overall problem management process. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/problem-management/problem-mgmt-properties.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: problem_task_analyst works on a problem task and manages it through its life cycle. It is not the default role allowed to re-analyze a completed problem.
problem_coordinator works on a problem or problem task, but the default value of the re-analyze property is problem_manager, which contains problem_coordinator rather than the other way round.
sn_problem_read gives read access to the Problem Management application and related records, so it cannot re-analyze a problem.

source.excerpt: This user can also administer problem properties, and this is the only role that could reopen a problem record. So someone serving as a manager would need this role.

questions.question: A problem coordinator assesses a new problem, decides it is valid and needs a resolution, and clicks Confirm. What happens to the problem state?

options.text: It moves to the Fix in Progress state
It moves to the Root Cause Analysis state
It stays in the Assess state until a task is assigned
It moves to the Known Error state

explanation.correct: When a problem is valid and requires a resolution, the coordinator clicks Confirm during assessment. After that confirmation, the problem enters the Root Cause Analysis state. The state model runs New, Assess, Root Cause Analysis, Fix in Progress, Resolved, and Closed. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/problem-management/assess-a-problem.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Fix in Progress comes later: during root cause analysis, clicking Fix changes the state to Fix in Progress so a change request can apply the permanent fix.
Confirm moves the problem out of Assess directly. The documentation states that the confirmation moves the problem to the Root Cause Analysis state, with no task needed first.

Known Error is one of the legacy states for existing customers (Open, Pending Change, Known Error, Closed or Resolved). The Madrid state model uses New, Assess, Root Cause Analysis, Fix in Progress, Resolved, and Closed.

source.excerpt: The life cycle for managing problems starts with detecting and logging them, then moving into investigation and diagnosis, and finally concluding with resolution and closure.

questions.question: No permanent fix exists yet for a problem, but the team has found a way for users to keep working. The coordinator fills in the Workaround field and clicks Communicate Workaround. What is the purpose of the workaround?

options.text: To record the permanent fix that removes the root cause
To lessen the impact until an actual resolution exists
To resolve and close every related incident in one step
To publish a known error article to the knowledge base

explanation.correct: ServiceNow defines a workaround as a temporary way to restore service failures and lessen the impact of a problem for which an actual resolution is not yet available. Communicating it notifies the related incidents that a workaround is available, so agents and users can keep working while root cause analysis and the permanent fix continue. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/problem-management/communicate-workaround.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: A workaround is temporary by definition. The permanent fix is documented separately and is usually applied through a change request before the problem is resolved.
Communicate Workaround copies the workaround to the related incidents' work notes and comments and sends notifications; it does not change their state to Resolved.
Known error articles are created with the separate Create Known Error Article related link. The legacy docs note that communicating a workaround does not create a knowledge article.

source.excerpt: Our goal in Problem Management is to identify the root cause of incidents, find feasible workarounds, and implement permanent solutions that prevent future occurrences.

questions.question: A problem is already open for a recurring network connectivity issue, and the service desk logs several new incidents describing the same issue. How should these incidents be handled?

options.text: Create a separate problem for each new incident
Add the incidents to the existing problem record
Create a problem task for each of the new incidents
Raise a change request from each of the incidents

explanation.correct: ServiceNow recommends adding multiple incidents to a problem to avoid creating multiple problems for incidents that have the same issue. On the problem, the Incidents related list has an Add button, and the selected incidents then appear under the Incidents tab. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/problem-management/add-multiple-incidents-to-problem.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Separate problems are what adding incidents to one problem is meant to avoid when the incidents have the same issue.
A problem task is created to initiate root cause analysis, for example by assigning a Root Cause Analysis task to a team. It is not used to link each incident.
A change request is raised from the problem once the root cause can be fixed. It is not how new incidents with the same issue are grouped.

source.excerpt: A problem can also arise when the same or similar incidents occur repeatedly, without a clear understanding of the root cause.

questions.question: A problem coordinator opens the Analysis Information section of a problem form to document what the investigation found. Which two of these fields are in that section? (Choose two)

options.text: Workaround
Fix notes
Cause notes
Resolved by

explanation.correct: The problem form documentation lists two fields under Analysis Information: Workaround, the method used to overcome the problem (which can be shared with Communicate Workaround), and Cause notes, which record what caused the problem. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/problem-management/problem-form.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Fix notes, describing how the problem was fixed, are under the Resolution Information section, not Analysis Information.
Resolved by is a read-only field under Resolution Information that shows the user who resolved the issue.

source.excerpt: The form has three tabs, Analysis Information, Resolution Information, and Other Information.

questions.question: A problem coordinator sets the Configuration item field on a new problem to a database server CI from the CMDB. According to the problem form, what does the class of that CI identify?

options.text: The priority, such as Critical or Planning
The type of problem, such as database
The state, such as Assess or Fix in Progress
The resolution code, such as Risk Accepted

explanation.correct: On the problem form, the Configuration item field holds the CI that the problem applies to, and the CI class of the selected configuration item identifies the type of problem, for example, hardware, network, or database. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/problem-management/problem-form.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Priority is read-only and is set according to the Impact and Urgency values, not by the CI class.
State is a read-only field whose value changes as the problem proceeds from one state to another. The CI class does not set it.
Resolution code indicates whether the problem is resolved, a fix is applied, a duplicate is available, or the coordinator accepts the risk. The CI class does not set it.

questions.question: An administrator needs a map of how the applications and hosts behind an online ordering service connect, so the impact of a failing component is visible. Which approach does Service Mapping use?

options.text: Horizontal discovery that lists each device independently
Top-down mapping of connections between devices and apps
Manual entry of each CI relationship by an administrator
Correlating third-party monitoring alerts with known CIs

explanation.correct: Service Mapping maps dependencies based on the connections between devices and applications, which ServiceNow calls top-down mapping. The resulting application service maps show infrastructure objects and the connections between them, so a faulty object appears together with the devices and applications it affects. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-operations-management/itom-visibility/itom-visibility-landing-page.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Horizontal discovery is what Discovery performs. It finds devices and applications but connections between them are not included, so it cannot show service impact.
Service Mapping builds maps automatically, mainly with discovery patterns, and can also use tags and traffic connections; it does not rely on manual relationship entry.
Correlating alerts from third-party monitoring tools with configuration items is ITOM AIOps, which consumes ITOM Visibility data rather than building service maps.

questions.question: A problem coordinator suspects that a failed database server is behind outages of an HR application. Which feature graphically shows the server along with the application and business services it supports?

options.text: CI Class Manager
Schema map
Dependency Views
Tables & Columns

explanation.correct: Dependency Views graphically displays an infrastructure view for a CI and the application or business services that it is part of and that it supports. The map can show both upstream and downstream dependencies for the root CI, and gives access to related incidents, problems, and changes. Note that from Brazil, Dependency Views is being prepared for future deprecation, with Unified Map as the newer experience. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/servicenow-platform/dependency-views/c_BusinesssServiceManagementMaps.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: CI Class Manager is used to view, create, or edit CI class definitions and class settings, not to map one CI to the services it supports.
A schema map shows parts of the database schema for a selected table. It does not show how a specific server supports business services.
Tables & Columns, under System Definition, is where you select a table to view its schema. It works with tables, not with CI relationships.

questions.question: Discovery has populated the CMDB with servers and applications, but an administrator still cannot see which of them depend on each other to deliver the payroll service. What explains this?

options.text: Discovery stores connections, but they are hidden by default
Discovery omits connections; Service Mapping maps them
Discovery finds network devices only, not the applications
Service Mapping replaces Discovery and ignores its CI results

explanation.correct: Discovery performs horizontal discovery: it identifies computers, servers, network devices and the applications running on them, but connections between devices and applications are not included. Service Mapping fills that gap with top-down mapping that maps dependencies based on those connections, and it builds on the results of horizontal discovery. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-operations-management/itom-visibility/itom-visibility-landing-page.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The docs state that connections between devices and applications are not included in horizontal discovery, so there is nothing hidden to reveal.
Discovery can find IP-enabled devices and the applications that run on them, as well as cloud resources and TLS certificates, not just network gear.
Service Mapping relies on Discovery and the MID Server and uses the results of horizontal discovery performed by Discovery, rather than replacing it.

questions.question: A problem coordinator creates a known error article from a problem and leaves the Attachment link check box cleared. How does the content of the article appear on the problem?

options.text: As an attachment on the problem record
As content in the problem work notes
As text copied into the Workaround field
As a result in the Related Search field

explanation.correct: On the known error article form, the Attachment link check box controls how the article shows on the problem. If it is selected, the article appears as an attachment in the problem record. If it is not selected, the content of the article appears in the work note of the problem. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/problem-management/known-error-article-form.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The article appears as an attachment only when the Attachment link check box is selected.
The Workaround field on the problem describes the method used to overcome the problem. Clearing Attachment link sends the article content to the work notes, not to this field.
Related Search shows knowledge articles found when the problem statement is updated. Clearing Attachment link puts the article content in the work notes.

questions.question: A problem coordinator sees that 15 incidents in the past month all involve the same failing printer, and no problem exists for them yet. Which step of the Problem Management workflow should come first?

options.text: Raise a change request to replace the printer
Create a problem to find the underlying cause
Publish a known error article for the printer
Accept the risk that it cannot be fixed now

explanation.correct: The Problem Management workflow starts with problem creation: you can create a problem to identify and permanently fix the underlying root cause when you have recurring incidents or after a major incident. Assessment, root cause analysis, communicating the outcome, and fixing follow. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/problem-management/exploring-problem-management.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: A change request comes after root cause analysis: if the root cause can be fixed, a change request is created from the problem and assigned to the relevant team.
In the workflow, a known error article is created when communicating the outcome, after the fix or workaround of the problem has been identified. That comes later than problem creation.
Accepting the risk is an option during root cause analysis when there is no permanent fix or not enough budget. It needs an existing problem.

questions.question: During root cause analysis, the team acknowledges a problem but has no permanent resolution for it, so the coordinator clicks Accept Risk. With default properties, what happens to the problem?

options.text: It moves to Resolved with the code Risk Accepted
It moves to Closed with the code Risk Accepted
It moves to Fix in Progress until a change is raised
It moves to Closed with the code Canceled

explanation.correct: Clicking Accept Risk sends the problem directly to the Closed or Resolved state with the resolution code Risk accepted. Which state it enters depends on the property Accept Risk moves the Problem to Closed state instead of Resolved state (problem.acceptrisk.move_to_closed), and the default value of that property is true. So the problem is closed. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/problem-management/investigate-root-cause.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Resolved is used only if problem.acceptrisk.move_to_closed is set to false. Its default value is true, so the problem goes to Closed.
Fix in Progress is the state set by clicking Fix when the problem can be resolved. Accept Risk is for when there is no permanent resolution.
Canceled is the resolution code recorded when a problem is canceled. Accepting the risk records the code Risk accepted.

questions.question: A service desk agent has an incident On Hold with the reason Awaiting Problem. Its linked problem is then resolved with the resolution code Fix Applied, using the Madrid problem state model. What happens to the incident?

options.text: It stays On Hold until an agent resolves it manually
It moves to In Progress so the assignee can verify the fix
It is set to Resolved with the code Resolved by problem
It receives the fix in work notes but stays On Hold

explanation.correct: With the Problem Management Best Practice - Madrid - State Model plugin, an incident that is On Hold with the reason Awaiting Problem is updated automatically when its problem is resolved or closed with Fix Applied. The incident state changes to Resolved, its resolution code becomes Resolved by problem, and the caller and assignee are emailed. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/problem-management/sync-btwn-inci-prob.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Manual resolution is not needed here. For incidents awaiting a problem, resolving the problem with Fix Applied sets the incident to Resolved automatically.
The documented outcome for an On Hold, Awaiting Problem incident is the Resolved state, not In Progress, when the problem is resolved with Fix Applied.
Copying the fix to work notes without changing state describes the Communicate Fix related link. Resolving the problem with Fix Applied also resolves the waiting incident.
